ch05.anchor: aged Huadiao, of the true first grade
ch05.note: Huadiao (花雕, ‘carved flowers’) is the finest grade of Shaoxing yellow rice-wine, matured for years in earthenware jars traditionally decorated with painted reliefs — hence the name. Amber, warm and mellow, it is the classic banqueting wine of the Chinese south, and a mark of a lavish table.

Lu Xiaofeng’s ‘mark’ is a huaya (花押), a personal cipher or monogram — a single character (here feng, ‘phoenix’) written in a private, unreproducible flourish and used, like a signet, to authenticate a message. That Zhu Ting will follow a stranger on sight of it is the whole force of the device: the sign is as good as the man’s own hand.

ch05.anchor: born in the year of the Goat
ch05.note: By the Chinese zodiac, each year belongs to one of twelve animals in fixed rotation, so a person’s birth-sign pins the year of their birth to within a twelve-year cycle. To say Shangguan Feiyan is ‘of the Goat’ and eighteen fixes her age exactly — which is why it can prove she cannot have a younger sister of twenty.

ch05.anchor: gets struck by a monk for a day
ch05.note: A pun built on a proverb. Zuo yi tian heshang, zhuang yi tian zhong (做一天和尚撞一天钟), ‘be a monk for a day and toll the bell for a day,’ means to do just the day’s bare duty and no more, drifting along as one is. Lu Xiaofeng turns it inside out: the courtesan is a ‘bell’ (zhong) for a day and is ‘struck’ (zhuang, which also carries a bawdy sense) by a monk for a day — making monk and courtesan the two halves of one daily office.

The joke rides on guisunzi (龟孙子), literally ‘turtle’s grandson,’ a coarse insult of the same tortoise-family as wangba (see the note in Chapter 1): a worthless wretch. Master Sun says that broke he is a turtle-spawn (guisunzi) and flush he is a great master (da laoye); since his surname happens to be Sun (孙, which also means ‘grandson’), the two collapse into his standing nickname.

ch05.anchor: the Shanglin Spring was famed near and far
ch05.note: The Shanglin Spring is a tavern; its named specialities are period fare. Bamboo-Leaf Green (竹叶青) is a pale-green Shanxi liquor steeped with bamboo leaves and herbs; the ‘twin-delicacy of fish and lamb’ is a dish, and a scholar’s pun besides — the character for a delicacy, xian (鲜), is written with ‘fish’ (鱼) beside ‘lamb’ (羊).

ch06.anchor: never let the golden cup stand empty to the moon
ch06.note: The two lines Lu Xiaofeng can sing — rensheng deyi xu jin huan, mo shi jinzun kong dui yue — open Li Bai’s ‘Bring in the Wine’ (将进酒), perhaps the most famous drinking-song in Chinese poetry: ‘When life goes well, drink your joy to the dregs; never let the golden cup face the moon empty.’ Li Bai (701–762), the great Tang poet and reputed drinker, made the carpe-diem toast a national commonplace; that these are the only lines Lu knows is the joke.

As the source states, the lyric is ascribed to Li Yu (李煜, 937–978), last ruler of the Southern Tang — a feeble king but a supreme poet — here mourning his first wife, Empress Zhou the Elder. ‘Endless Longing’ (长相思) is not a title but the name of a fixed tune-pattern, or ci, to which such lyrics were composed; the words fit a melody the reader is meant to hear behind them.

Hua Manlou is quoting a proverb, jinzhao you jiu jinzhao zui (今朝有酒今朝醉), ‘if there is wine today, then get drunk today’ — live for the moment and let tomorrow look to itself. It answers Lu Xiaofeng’s Li Bai lines with the same seize-the-day resignation, darker for the grief beneath it.

ch06.anchor: from Yanbei all the way into Shanxi
ch06.note: Yanbei (燕北), ‘north of Yan,’ is the old northern frontier country around and beyond present-day Beijing; Shanxi lies south and west of it. The span names the road they have travelled — down out of the far north toward the Guanzhong heartland where Yan Tieshan’s jewel-house stands — and marks how long Lu Xiaofeng has gone clean-shaven, fretting his moustache back.
